analysis.one_liner: Narrows which streams and wetlands the Clean Water Act protects.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase a 2015 rule that expanded federal pollution protections to smaller streams and nearby wetlands, and rewrite the Clean Water Act so federal rules apply only to waters that are navigable or continuously connected to navigable waters. Headwater streams, intermittent channels, and isolated wetlands would lose protection. It was referred to a House committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners and businesses that would otherwise need federal permits to pollute, fill, or build over smaller streams and wetlands — including farm operations, real estate developers, and energy and mining companies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, farm operations, energy and mining firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill would give no force or effect to the EPA-Army 'Clean Water Rule' signed May 27, 2015, which defined the scope of federally protected waters. [S2] [S3]
It would limit Clean Water Act coverage to waters navigable-in-fact and permanent or continuously flowing streams, rivers, lakes, and oceans connected to navigable waters. [S2] [S3]

It would exclude from federal protection intermittent or ephemeral channels (such as rain-drainage channels) and wetlands — including playa lakes, prairie potholes, wet meadows, and vernal pools — that lack a continuous surface water connection, and bar counting such waters together to establish protection. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Communities downstream of newly unprotected waters: smaller streams and wetlands filter pollution and feed the rivers and reservoirs that supply drinking water, so their loss of protection shifts cleanup costs and water-quality risk to the public. Supporters argued the existing rule created uncertainty and overreach for landowners.

drawbacks.text: Removing federal protection for intermittent streams and unconnected wetlands would let those waters be polluted, filled, or developed without Clean Water Act permits, even though many of them drain into the rivers and reservoirs that supply drinking water downstream. [S2] [S3]
Prohibiting regulators from aggregating separate waters would make it harder to protect ecosystems that function as a connected whole rather than as isolated waters. [S2] [S3]

The bill's own premise — 'regulatory certainty' — was the stated rationale for the narrower definition, which backers said would reduce permit costs and land-use restrictions; an honest supporter would acknowledge that the lower cost comes from removing environmental oversight of the excluded waters. [S1] [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would reduce permit requirements and land-use restrictions for landowners and developers, which supporters framed as certainty. The cost falls on downstream water quality: the excluded waters are the headwaters and wetlands that feed larger rivers and reservoirs, so weakening oversight of them transfers pollution risk and cleanup costs to the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which routed it to its water resources subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the bill on June 9, 2015, with no cosponsors. [S4] [S5]
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced. [S5]
The next day it was referred to the subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and the committee never reported it to the full House. [S5]
The Congress ended January 3, 2017 with the bill never having received a floor vote in either chamber. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, federal Clean Water Rule protections over smaller streams and wetlands remained in place during the 114th Congress, and the land developers, farm operations, and energy and mining interests the bill was written to relieve never received the narrower definition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Clean water rules; developers and industry got no relief

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the Clean Water Rule and narrow the Clean Water Act definition of navigable waters.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors in either party.

industries.note: A narrower definition of protected waters means fewer federal permits and restrictions when filling or building over streams and wetlands, cutting project costs. The public bears the water-quality risk downstream.
Farm ditches, intermittent channels, and prairie pothole wetlands would be explicitly excluded from Clean Water Act jurisdiction, reducing oversight of farm runoff and wetland conversion.
Discharges into ephemeral streams and unconnected wetlands would no longer require federal pollution permits, lowering compliance costs for extraction and energy operations.

industries.industry: Municipal water utilities and downstream water users
industries.note: Unprotected headwater streams and filter wetlands feed drinking-water sources, so lost upstream oversight raises treatment and cleanup burdens for water systems and their ratepayers.
